1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: In that corridor, Mervyn Aloysius Fonseca knew more law than any man standing there. He had typed ten thousand orders with his own hands. Ten thousand. And not one of them carried his name.
1.sfx_cue: court corridor voices and shuffling files

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: Today, for the first time in fifteen years, somebody was going to call him sir. And that one word would destroy his life.

1.speaker: SENIOR COUNSEL
1.text: No no no. Delete that whole paragraph. The application was dismissed, not disposed. From the top.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Sir, yesterday's order is saying disposed. I typed it myself.

1.speaker: SENIOR COUNSEL
1.text: Yesterday's order was mine. This one is also mine. Your job is the machine, not the meaning.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Let me finish the citations only. I can sit inside till lunch.

1.speaker: SENIOR COUNSEL
1.text: You can sit outside till I call. Client is coming.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Six pages I have already typed.

1.speaker: SENIOR COUNSEL
1.text: And for six pages you have been paid. Kindly close the door from that side.

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: Fifteen years back, the bar council had thrown him out. No degree, they said. Not a real advocate, they said. He still came to that court every single morning. He simply came carrying typing paper instead of a file.
1.sfx_cue: door opening onto crowded court corridor

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: Oye. Move from the chamber door. Advocates that side, litigants near the railing.
1.sfx_cue: court corridor voices and shuffling files

1.speaker: morris
1.text: I am attached to this chamber.

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: Attached? Then your chair also must be attached, no? Go and sit on it.

1.speaker: VOICE IN CORRIDOR
1.text: Attached, he is saying! Arre, maybe he is the stapler!

1.speaker: morris
1.text: One day this record will show who knows the work in this building.

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: The record is showing one typist blocking my corridor. Shall I write that also?

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: Forty-three years old. Twenty-two years inside that building. And in front of thirty people, he was standing there with a bundle of paper, being told where to put his chair.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Sir. Sir, please. Urgent matters you are hearing today?

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Who sent you here?

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Registry sent me up. Upstairs sent me down. Since ten fifteen I am going up-down, up-down, sir. Nobody is even looking at my face.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: What is the matter?

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: My mother's room, sir. Landlord has put a new lock this morning. Her medicines are inside only. Her BP tablets, sir. She is sitting on the landing since nine o'clock.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: You have an advocate?

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: He is asking twelve hundred before he even opens the file. Twelve hundred, sir. I am having four hundred and sixty. That also is my mother's.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Then go to legal aid.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: They gave me one token. Sixty-eight. Board is still showing twenty-three. By evening they will close and she will sleep on that landing.

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: Arre, don't waste your time with him. Can't you see, he himself has been sent out to wait?

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Sent out... from inside the chamber?

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: Haan! Along with the other furniture!

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: And the whole corridor laughed. Advocates. Clerks. Litigants. Even the man selling tea stopped pouring, to laugh.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Bas.

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: Ji, sir. Certainly, sir. Whatever you order, sir.

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: That was the joke. That everybody laughed at. That he should ever order anything.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Boy. Give the file here.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Landlord is saying agreement finished on the first. My mother is saying he took three months advance. Receipt is not there.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: And the lock he changed today itself?

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Nine o'clock, sir.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Show me his notice. This notice is giving seven days. Delivered yesterday. And he broke the lock this morning.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Meaning?

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Meaning your landlord has already broken his own paper. This affidavit has no verification. This application is asking final relief as interim relief. Who drafted this rubbish?

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: One man near the photocopy shop. Sir... can it be heard or not?

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Not like this.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Then you tell me how! Please, sir. Whatever you say, exactly that I will write. Ten seconds you looked at that file. Ten seconds. That advocate is holding it since two months.

1.speaker: COURT CLERK
1.text: Ei ei ei! What are you doing! Get up!

1.speaker: morris
1.text: Get up. Get up, I am saying.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: No sir. Not until you are saying yes.

1.speaker: morris
1.text: People are watching.

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Let them watch!

1.speaker: irfan
1.text: Sir. Hear the case.

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: Thirty people were watching. Ten minutes ago they were laughing at him. And now a man was on the floor, holding his feet, calling him sir.

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: Mervyn did not correct him. He did not say, I am only a typist. He did not say, they threw me out fifteen years back.

1.speaker: NARRATOR
1.text: He said nothing at all. And in that silence, a court was born that no country in the world had ever created.

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: One page. No case number. No seal. No court behind it. That is all it took — and by evening, a man who had refused for two months would open a lock and count out six thousand rupees.
2.sfx_cue: crowded court corridor, files thudding on bench

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Sir, hear the case. Just once. My mother is still sitting outside that locked room.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Take your hands away from my feet.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Say you will hear it.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: I am not hearing anything. Get up.

2.speaker: COURT CLERK
2.text: Your lordship! Shall we clear the corridor for this historic sitting?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: You have shouted enough for one morning.

2.speaker: COURT CLERK
2.text: And you have been promoted very quickly for one morning.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Come with me.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Inside the chamber, sir?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: No. The copying room.

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: The copying room. Not the chamber. Twenty-two years in that building, and there was still only one room he was allowed to enter without permission.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Listen carefully. This is only advice. You will not call it an order.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Yes, sir.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: You will not tell anybody that I heard a case.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: No, sir.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: And stop calling me sir every second sentence.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Yes... sorry.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Give me the landlord's notice.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Here. He has written that we abandoned the room. My mother has slept there nine years, sir. Nine years.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: The notice is giving seven days. When was it delivered?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Yesterday afternoon.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Then he broke his own period. His own paper, and he could not wait for it.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Can you write that? Exactly that?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: I can write many things. Whether a fool obeys the paper is a different question.

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: Mervyn put one clean sheet into the machine. And his fingers found the form. The same form he had typed ten thousand times. For other men.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Upon perusal of the application... no. Upon perusal of the material placed on record.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: What material?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Your file. Do not interrupt the record.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Sorry.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: It appears that possession was disturbed during the subsistence of the notice period.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Sir, will he even understand this language?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: He will understand the next sentence.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: The respondent is directed to restore access forthwith, failing which further proceedings shall follow.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Further proceedings where?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Do you want your mother's key, or a lecture on jurisdiction?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: The key.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Then let the sentence do its work.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: But there is no stamp, sir.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: A stamp impresses people who cannot read. Your landlord can read.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: And the signature?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: The signature tells him somebody is prepared to continue.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Prepared as what?

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: And there it was. The whole crime. Not a forged seal. Not a stolen file. Four words, in his own handwriting.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Presiding officer.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Sir... which office?

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Do not ask a question when you are afraid of its answer.

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: That afternoon, Irfan carried one page to a hardware shop.
2.sfx_cue: metal shop shutter rattling, traffic nearby

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: What is this?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: A direction to restore possession forthwith.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: From which court? There is no case number on this.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Read the last line.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: Further proceedings shall follow.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Yes.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: Who has signed it?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: The officer hearing the matter.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: Hearing it where?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: You can go and ask him yourself. I will tell him you refused.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: Arre, there is no need to become dramatic. I changed the lock only to protect the property.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: My mother is outside on the landing.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: Take the spare key. I am obeying under protest.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: And the three months advance?

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: You people learn one legal phrase and immediately you become advocates.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: The notice itself is saying he received it.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: How much?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Six thousand rupees.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: I will deduct electricity.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: There is no electricity bill pending.

2.speaker: LANDLORD
2.text: Fine. Six thousand. Sign here and get out of my shop.
2.sfx_cue: cash notes counted on metal counter

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: No case number. No seal. No court anywhere behind that page. And the landlord paid every single rupee.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: He obeyed every line, sir. Every line!

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Lower your voice.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: He returned the key. He returned the advance. My mother touched that paper to her forehead.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: I told you. It was advice.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Advice is not returning six thousand rupees.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Then what do you think it was?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: A judgment.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Do not use words you do not understand.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: I understand what opened that door.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: And what have you brought in that envelope?

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Four hundred and sixty rupees. Everything I was having yesterday.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: Take it back.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: Then call it filing fees.

2.speaker: morris
2.text: There was no filing.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: There will be now.

2.speaker: FIRST MAN
2.text: Sir. Irfan is saying you hear urgent property matters.

2.speaker: SECOND MAN
2.text: We have brought our files.

2.speaker: irfan
2.text: And they have brought their fees.
2.sfx_cue: two cash envelopes placed beside the files

2.speaker: NARRATOR
2.text: Two files. Two envelopes. Yesterday he was furniture in a corridor. Tomorrow, he would need a room.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: Five thousand rupees. That is what it costs to build a court in this country. One second-hand table. Eight inches of wood. One board with gold letters. And one girl who has never seen a courtroom in her life.

3.speaker: FIRST MAN
3.text: Sir, my brother sold our father's sewing machines without asking me. I need an order before he sells the shop also.

3.speaker: SECOND MAN
3.text: Mine is a salary matter. Three months unpaid. Irfan is saying you finish quickly.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: I have not accepted either matter.

3.speaker: irfan
3.text: They have come because the first order worked.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: That was not an order.

3.speaker: FIRST MAN
3.text: Then write me the same kind of not-order.

3.speaker: SECOND MAN
3.text: Five hundred I can pay now. Another five hundred after recovery.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: This is a public canteen. Put that money away.

3.speaker: FIRST MAN
3.text: Then where should we put it? Irfan said your office is upstairs.

3.speaker: irfan
3.text: I said he works upstairs. I did not say he has an office.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Bas. Both of you, wait till evening. Bring every agreement, receipt and notice you are having.

3.speaker: FIRST MAN
3.text: And where will you hear us, sir?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: You will be informed.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: He did not take the envelopes on the table. He took them under it. Where dignity could pretend not to see.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: Five days after a stranger touched his feet, Mervyn Aloysius Fonseca climbed a metal staircase above a tyre shop.
3.sfx_cue: air wrench bursts, metal staircase creaking

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Mind the second step. It bends when heavy people are using it.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: You said the room has a separate entrance.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: It is having. Nobody enters through the tyres unless they fall through the floor.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: There is grease on the wall.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Downstairs also there is grease. That is how a tyre shop is earning money.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Clients must be able to wait outside.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Clients? You told me typing work.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Documentation. Consultations. Settlement of private disputes.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Advocate work?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: No.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Write the receipt.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Occupation?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Dispute resolution.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: That is not an occupation.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: It is now.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: By noon, one carpenter had put a second-hand dining table on a platform eight inches high. Not one foot. Eight inches. Enough to look up at. Cheap enough to afford.

3.speaker: CARPENTER
3.text: If you lean on the left side, the whole thing will salute you.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Brace it underneath.

3.speaker: CARPENTER
3.text: That is costing two hundred more.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: It costs nothing if you had built it straight.

3.speaker: CARPENTER
3.text: Straight wood is costing more than crooked wood, sir.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Do it.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: At two o'clock, a sign painter carried in a black board with gold letters.

3.speaker: SIGN PAINTER
3.text: Arbitration and Dispute Resolution Forum. Exactly as you have written.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: The word forum is smaller than the others.

3.speaker: SIGN PAINTER
3.text: You paid for twenty-four letters. This is having thirty-seven.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: And the line below?

3.speaker: SIGN PAINTER
3.text: Presiding Officer. That is large enough to read from the tyre shop.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Make sir smaller.

3.speaker: SIGN PAINTER
3.text: There is no sir on the board.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: I said officer. Make officer smaller.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: He was thinking that word so loudly, it came out of his mouth.

3.speaker: SIGN PAINTER
3.text: You said— never mind. Give me fifty rupees for correction.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Hang it straight first.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: What is this board?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: It states the work conducted here.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: You told me typing.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Documents will be typed.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Police will come for dispute resolution?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Only if tyres are sold without receipts.

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Your board is very handsome, sir. Please conduct all resolutions upstairs.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: That was the first time the tyre shop owner called him sir. Mervyn paid the sign painter without bargaining.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: A dais? You have bought a dais before buying groceries?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: There is rice for three days.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: There is rice. There is no oil. There is no dal. But somewhere above a tyre shop, there is a dais.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: It is an office expense.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: Say the office name properly.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Arbitration and Dispute Resolution Forum.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: And who appointed you to it?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Private parties appoint an arbitrator by consent.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: Did these parties consent?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: They brought files and fees.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: That is not what I asked you.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: The record will reflect consent.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: What record?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: The one I am creating.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: And who is keeping this record?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: A clerk.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: You are having a clerk now?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: I will have one tomorrow.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: With whose salary?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: The forum's fees.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: Mervyn. Look at me. Is this a court?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: No. It is a lawful private forum.

3.speaker: vaishali
3.text: Then why is it needing a dais?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Because people obey a raised table.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Sir, I was told there is a clerk vacancy?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Who told you?

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: The sign painter, sir. He is my mother's neighbour. He said you paid on time.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Have you worked in an office before?

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: No, sir. Twelfth standard I finished. I can read English, type slowly, and make tea quickly.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Tea is not part of the designation.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: There is a designation?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Registry clerk.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Registry... like a court registry?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Like a private forum registry.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Will I have to wear a uniform, sir?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: No. Plain clothes. Clean file work. You will maintain the register and call matters by number.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: I don't... I have never called a matter, sir.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Say — matter number one, parties to enter.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Matter number one, parties to enter.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Louder. People waiting near an air compressor must hear you.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Matter number one, parties to enter!

3.speaker: TYRE SHOP OWNER
3.text: Very respectable. Even my customers are frightened.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: What is the salary, sir?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Three thousand rupees per month. Paid on the last working day.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Three thousand... every month?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: If the register is correct.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: My father is getting two thousand six hundred, sir. Night security.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Your father's salary is not before this forum.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: Sorry, sir.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Read this appointment acknowledgment. Sign at the bottom.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: It is saying... I certify the proceedings recorded by me.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: That is standard language.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: What proceedings, sir?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: The matters you call. The appearances. The documents filed.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: And if I am spelling something wrong?

3.speaker: morris
3.text: You correct it before signing.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: My mother will not believe this. Nobody in our family has ever had a desk job.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Then give her something respectable to believe.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: At four thirty, Sarika Kamble opened a new register. Mervyn wrote one on the first page, and two on the second.

3.speaker: morris
3.text: Nobody knows this address yet.

3.speaker: sarika
3.text: The two matters are finished for today, sir.

3.speaker: STRANGER
3.text: I am not one of the two.

3.speaker: STRANGER
3.text: I need the presiding officer.

3.speaker: NARRATOR
3.text: Two days that board had been hanging. Two days. And already, somebody had come who was not sent.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: Till today, every paper he signed had helped somebody. A locked room opened. A stolen advance returned. Today, a builder walks in — and after today, Mervyn Aloysius Fonseca will never be able to say that again.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Do not put that file in any queue. The land is worth one crore forty lakh, and I need an order by Friday.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: Sir, he walked straight inside. I told him there is a registry process.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: There is. Sit down. Both of you.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: I prefer standing. The seller took two lakh from me, signed an agreement, and now he wants to sell elsewhere.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: What do you want from this forum?

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Specific performance. Possession. Registration at the agreed price of thirty-one lakh.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: You said the land is worth one crore forty.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: That is exactly why Friday is important.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: No. Notice must be served. The other party must consent to arbitration.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: The agreement is containing an arbitration clause.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: An arbitration clause is not consent to whichever room you choose.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Then persuade him this is the correct room.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: I do not persuade parties. I hear them.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Of course, sir. Of course. Your shop is above rented premises, isn't it? A long dispute with that landlord would be very inconvenient.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: That is how a threat sounds when the man making it has money. No shouting. Just a small observation about somebody else's rent.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: Sir... should I go outside?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: No. You are the registry clerk. Record that the applicant requested an urgent hearing.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: What case number, sir?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Case number zero zero three of two thousand twenty-two.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Friday. Eleven in the morning.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: You will not fix my hearing.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Certainly not, sir. I will merely bring everybody at the useful time.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: Friday came with two witnesses, one very reluctant seller, and one advocate old enough to distrust clean paper.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: Case number zero zero three of two thousand twenty-two. Applicant versus respondent. All parties come inside.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: This is the court? Above a tyre shop?

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Do not answer anything yet. Let me see the board.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: You received notice. You came with counsel. Please do not waste the presiding officer's time.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Presiding over what?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Counsel, take your seat.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: I have practised thirty-eight years. I stand until I know before whom I am appearing.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Then remain standing, and read clause fourteen of your client's agreement.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: I have read it.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Read it aloud.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Any dispute arising from this agreement shall be referred to arbitration by a sole arbitrator mutually accepted by both parties.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Good. Is your client disputing the agreement?

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: I dispute the price. Thirty-one lakh is robbery now.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: It was not robbery when he took my two lakh.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: That was a token. I... I said I would return it.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Did you return it?

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: Not yet.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Did you send written cancellation?

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: No.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Did you accept another offer?

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Sir, that question concerns a separate negotiation.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Then the answer is yes.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: They offered ninety-eight lakh.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: There. He admits it.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: He admits receiving an offer. He does not admit this forum has jurisdiction.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Your client came after notice. He filed a reply through you. He is arguing the merits.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Appearance is not appointment.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Correct. Sarika — give both parties the consent memorandum.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: Sir, the blue copy or the white copy?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: The white copy. Blue remains in registry.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: You prepared consent forms before we entered?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: A competent registry prepares for foreseeable objections.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: He was not faking a court. He was collecting signatures that would make his room legal. And the old advocate was about to hand him one.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: What happens if I do not sign?

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Then the advance dispute continues, the other purchaser waits, and your title remains questioned.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Do not instruct my client.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Counsel. Advise him. I will give you ten minutes.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: And if we sign, you will hear us fully?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Every document. Every objection. On record.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: I want that sentence written into the memorandum.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Sarika, add it.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: Every document and... every objection will be heard on record.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: Ten minutes became twenty-three. Then the old advocate came back with both signatures.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: My client consents to this arbitration. That is not an admission on the merits.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Recorded. Now show me why an agreement taken at thirty-one lakh should disappear when the value rises.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Because the applicant was required to pay the balance within sixty days.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Did he offer payment?

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: He sent three letters.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: And a banker's cheque for twenty-nine lakh.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: I did not deposit it.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: That was your choice. His obligation was to tender payment.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: The agreement also required title clearance.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Which your client delayed by withholding the original property card.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: Who told you that?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Your own reply. Paragraph nine.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: I... let me see that.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: You drafted it.

4.speaker: VOICE IN ROOM
4.text: Arre! The advocate has written against his own client!

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Silence. This is not a tea stall.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: No. It is a hearing. Continue with your objection.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: There is no further factual objection.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Then the hearing is closed.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: For forty minutes, Mervyn typed the largest order he had ever put beneath his own signature.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: The respondent shall accept the balance of twenty-nine lakh and execute the conveyance within seven days.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Until registration, the respondent shall create no third-party interest in the land.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: And if I refuse?

4.speaker: morris
4.text: Your signed consent and this award will accompany the applicant's enforcement petition.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: I am having the banker's cheque right here.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Give it to me. My client will acknowledge receipt.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: You are telling me to obey him? In front of everybody?

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: I am telling you that you signed the agreement, accepted arbitration, and lost on the documents.

4.speaker: LANDOWNER
4.text: Then write that I am taking the cheque under the award.

4.speaker: sarika
4.text: I will record it, sir.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: Record this also. My client will execute the conveyance within seven days.

4.speaker: dhawale
4.text: Thank you, sir. A very useful order. Exactly when required.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: The order follows the record. Not your requirement.

4.speaker: NARRATOR
4.text: He was telling the truth. The contract was real. The breach was real. The order was correct in every line. And a man who threatened him had just bought one crore forty lakh of land for thirty-one.

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: One matter remains.

4.speaker: morris
4.text: What matter?

4.speaker: advocate
4.text: May I see the order appointing you as arbitrator?

5.speaker: NARRATOR
5.text: To keep a fake court alive, you need one thing above everything else. You need to know which cases the real court has not got. And that list exists. In one room. In one cupboard. Guarded by one clerk who does not want money.

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: Sit down, Mr Fonseca. I did not ask that question in front of my client for a reason.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Then ask it now.

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: Is there an appointment order?

5.speaker: morris
5.text: There is a consent memorandum signed by both parties.

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: That is not what I asked you.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: No. There is no prior appointment order.

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: Thirty-eight years I am practising. Do you know how many rooms like yours I have seen?

5.speaker: morris
5.text: How many?

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: Four. All four closed within one year. Not because they were caught. Because one losing party went to a real court, and the real court said — which case? Which number? Which judge?

5.speaker: morris
5.text: My orders are correct on the documents.

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: Your orders are excellent. That is the tragedy. If you had a degree you would be sitting in that building, and I would be standing before you.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Is that a compliment or a warning?

5.speaker: advocate
5.text: It is arithmetic. Today I consented because my client had already lost. The next lawyer will not consent. He will check first.

5.speaker: NARRATOR
5.text: And that was the sentence that changed everything. Not a threat. Not a police complaint. One old man, being kind. He will check first.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Pandit-ji. One minute.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Arre, Mervyn. Long time. They are saying you have started some office.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: A private forum. Small matters.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Small matters. Above a tyre shop. With a board.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: You have seen it.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Everybody in this registry has seen it. What do you want?

5.speaker: morris
5.text: The civil pending list.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: The pending list.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Only to see which disputes are already filed here. I do not want to touch a matter that is before a real judge.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: You do not want conflict. Very responsible.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: It is thirty-two pages. One hour.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: It is thirty-two pages of other people's misfortune, and you want to shop in it.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Name your price.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Put that back inside.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Two thousand.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: I said put it back. Cash is evidence. Cash is a number somebody can count in a court.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Then what do you want?

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Come at one o'clock. Everybody goes for lunch at one.

5.speaker: NARRATOR
5.text: At one o'clock, the registry emptied. And a thirty-two page list was left lying on the rear photocopier. Not handed over. Just left. So that nobody had given anything to anybody.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Page eleven is missing.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Page eleven is land acquisition. Government matters. You will not survive government matters.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: You have read it before leaving it.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: I have read every page in that cupboard for nineteen years. Nobody has ever asked me one question about any of them.

5.speaker: NARRATOR
5.text: Nineteen years. And Mervyn understood, standing in that empty room, that he was not the only man in that building who had been made invisible.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: It is done. Thirty-two pages.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Good. Now my price.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: You said not money.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: It is not money.

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: One sealed envelope. Every month. On the last working day, same day you pay your clerk.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Containing what?

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: You will open it first. And then you will do what is inside it.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: Pandit-ji—

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: No questions. That is the price. No questions, ever, about what is in the envelope or who put it there.

5.speaker: morris
5.text: And if I refuse?

5.speaker: pandit
5.text: Then give back the photographs and we will both forget this lunch hour.

5.speaker: NARRATOR
5.text: He had come to buy a list, so that he would never rule on a case somebody could check. He walked out owing a man twelve rulings he had not yet written.

5.speaker: NARRATOR
5.text: And the first envelope would arrive on the last working day of that same month.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: Eleven years. For eleven years, Manjula Gaikwad had stood outside her own father's gate and asked her brother for the key. Eleven years of no. And then, in eight days, a room above a tyre shop gave her what the law had never bothered to.

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: Sir, they told me you are giving dates quickly. Is it true?

6.speaker: morris
6.text: What is the matter?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: Land, sir. My father's land. Four acres. My name is there in the record, equal share. My brother is having both keys.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Since when?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: Since my father died. Eleven years.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Have you filed anywhere?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: One advocate took nine thousand rupees. Three years he took dates. Then he stopped picking up the phone.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: And the crop income for these eleven years?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: He is saying there is no income. Sir, I am standing at that gate every harvest. I am counting the trolleys.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: You have counted them?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: Eleven years I am counting. It is written. In my own hand.
6.sfx_cue: cloth bag opening, notebook placed on desk

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: One school notebook. Eleven harvests. Every trolley that left that field, written by a woman standing at a gate she was not allowed to open.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Sarika. Register this matter. Hearing on the eighth day.

6.speaker: sarika
6.text: Eight days, sir?

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Eight days.

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: Sir... eight days?

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Is that a problem?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: No, sir. It is only that... my last date was after fourteen months. And then it was cancelled.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: Eight days later, Bhaskar Gaikwad walked up a metal staircase. Not because he was summoned. Because his sister had told the whole lane there was a hearing, and not coming would look like fear.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: This is the forum? I thought it would be bigger.

6.speaker: sarika
6.text: Matter number nine of two thousand twenty-three. Parties to enter.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: You are the respondent?

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: I am her brother.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Both can be true. Is your sister's name in the seven-twelve extract?

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: It is there. But she is married. She is living in another village.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Does the record say — equal share, subject to marriage?

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: It does not say.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Then it says equal share. Who has been cultivating?

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: I am cultivating. Alone. Since eleven years, with my own hands.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: And the income?

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: There is no income. Cotton has failed. Everybody knows cotton has failed.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Every year for eleven years?

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: Ask any farmer.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: I am asking you. Your sister has produced a count of the trolleys that left that field. Two thousand nineteen — thirty-one trolleys. Two thousand twenty — twenty-eight.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: She is sitting at a gate writing in a notebook. That is not accounts.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: You are correct. It is not accounts. Where are the accounts?

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Eleven years of cultivation, and you have not brought one receipt, one weighing slip, one society entry.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: I did not know I had to bring.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: You knew there was a hearing about crop income.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: And the whole room was quiet. Because everybody in that room had a brother, or was one.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: This forum finds that the applicant holds an equal recorded share, and has been excluded from possession for eleven years without any accounting.

6.speaker: morris
6.text: The respondent shall deliver both keys and permit access according to her recorded share. He shall not lease the western half pending final accounting.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: Both keys?

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Both keys.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: And if I am not giving?

6.speaker: morris
6.text: Then this order and your presence today will accompany her petition, and you will explain to a longer forum why you brought no accounts.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: He was not frightened of the paper. He was frightened of the room. Fourteen people from his own lane, watching him be asked a question he could not answer.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: Take them.

6.speaker: bhaskar
6.text: And do not make a procession of this.

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: You made me beg at that gate for eleven years. Today, they will all hear.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: She walked down that metal staircase holding two keys, into a lane where every door was open.
6.sfx_cue: metal staircase, lane sounds, doors opening

6.speaker: LANE WOMAN
6.text: Manjula? Who gave the order?

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: Listen. All of you. Listen.

6.speaker: manjula
6.text: A court finally listened to me.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: It was not a court. There was no court. And in that whole lane, standing in that whole crowd, only one person knew it — and he was not there.

6.speaker: NARRATOR
6.text: Remember this day. Because in eleven episodes from now, a police officer will ask Mervyn Aloysius Fonseca to say that this order was worthless.

7.speaker: NARRATOR
7.text: Every empire built on paper dies the same way. Not by police. Not by a rival. By one man, at one desk, whose only job is to check that a number is real.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Sir, this bundle came in the afternoon filing. There is one attachment I cannot place.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Which attachment?

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: An award, sir. From some forum. The party has annexed it as proof of settled possession.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Read the cause title.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Arbitration and Dispute Resolution Forum. Before the Presiding Officer. Case number A-D-R-F, slash, one seven six, slash, twenty-three.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: One seven six. Meaning they are claiming one hundred and seventy-six matters.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Is that a problem, sir?

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: It is a number. Numbers are either true or they are not.

7.speaker: NARRATOR
7.text: Harshad Kotak had been sitting at that desk twenty-two years. In twenty-two years, he had signed nothing, decided nothing, and refused nothing that was correct. His entire profession was one question. Is this document what it says it is?

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Check the list of arbitrators empanelled with this court.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Checking, sir... no such name.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Check the section-eleven appointments. Last five years.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: No, sir.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Check the retired list. Sometimes they continue as arbitrators privately.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Sir, there is no such name anywhere.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: And the case-number sequence? A-D-R-F.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: This court is not issuing that series, sir. No court in this district is issuing that series.

7.speaker: NARRATOR
7.text: One hundred and seventy-six matters. From a forum that did not exist. Filed into a real court, by people who had no idea.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Shall I return the bundle at the counter, sir? Defective annexure.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: No.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Sir?

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: If I return it at the counter, the party will remove that annexure and file again by evening. And then it is gone.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Then... report it, sir? To the district judge?

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Report what? That one annexure has a number I do not recognise? He will ask me how many such awards exist. And I will say — I do not know, sir. One.

7.speaker: NARRATOR
7.text: This is why it survived five years. Not because nobody noticed. Because the first man who noticed knew that one paper is not a case.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Route it for scrutiny. Do not return it. Do not mark it defective.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: And if the party asks?

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: The party will not ask. People who file a fake award never ask why it is taking time.

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Tomorrow. First I want to see whether that number appears again.

7.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
7.text: Where will you keep it, sir?

7.speaker: hardik
7.text: Not the file. Only the number.

7.speaker: NARRATOR
7.text: He wrote A-D-R-F, slash, one seven six, slash, twenty-three on a slip of paper. He put it in his drawer. And he waited.
7.sfx_cue: pen on paper, drawer sliding shut

7.speaker: NARRATOR
7.text: Above a tyre shop, four kilometres away, Sarika Kamble called matter number one hundred and seventy-nine. Nobody in that room had ever heard the name Harshad Kotak.

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: Fourteen months. Fourteen salary envelopes. And Sarika Kamble had never once asked what she was signing — because for the first time in her family's history, somebody had given her a designation.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Matter number one hundred and eighty-two. Parties to enter.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Before we begin. I have one preliminary matter.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: You are appearing again, counsel.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: I am appearing under protest, and I have told my client so in writing.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: Noted. What is the preliminary matter?

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Not for you, sir. For your registry clerk.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Me?

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Madam. On every certified copy issued from this room, there is one line above your signature. Can you read it out for me?

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: I certify the proceedings recorded by me.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Thank you. Now tell me — what does certify mean?

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: It means... it is correct, sir. What is written is what happened.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: And who has authorised you to certify anything?

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Sir...

8.speaker: morris
8.text: Counsel, address the forum, not my staff.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: I am addressing the only person in this room whose signature travels outside it.

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: And that was true. His signature stayed on the paper. Hers went out. To landlords. To brothers. To builders. Into filings. Into a district court registry, four kilometres away, where a man had already written one number on a slip.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Sir, I will ask you the same question I asked in that back room. Where is the order appointing you?

8.speaker: morris
8.text: The parties consent.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: The parties consent to an arbitrator. Who made you one?

8.speaker: morris
8.text: I constituted this forum.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Say it fully.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: I constituted this forum myself. There is no external order appointing me as presiding officer.

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: He said it out loud. In his own room. In front of his own clerk. And the strange thing was — not one party got up and left.

8.speaker: advocate
8.text: Madam. Now you have heard it. Do you still certify?

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: That evening, after everybody had gone, Sarika did not go home.
8.sfx_cue: room emptying, door closing, fan alone

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Fourteen.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: What are you counting?

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Envelopes, sir. Fourteen months I am taking salary from this office.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: Your work has been correct. Every register entry.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: My father is a night watchman, sir. Twenty-eight years, one company. When they gave him a uniform, he wore it to a wedding.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: Sarika—

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: I told everybody. My mother. My aunt. The whole chawl. Sarika is working in a registry. Sarika is a registry clerk.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: That was not a lie.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Then what was it, sir?

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: He had an answer for the advocate. He had an answer for the builder. He had an answer for his own wife. He did not have one for this.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: That first day. I asked you what proceedings. You remember?

8.speaker: morris
8.text: I remember.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: And you said — that is standard language.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: It is standard language.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Sir. Do not call me by my name now. Just answer one thing.

8.speaker: morris
8.text: Ask.

8.speaker: sarika
8.text: Can I be jailed for this?

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: He was still thinking of the answer when she picked up her bag and walked down the metal staircase.
8.sfx_cue: bag lifted, footsteps on metal stairs

8.speaker: NARRATOR
8.text: And in a drawer, four kilometres away, the number A-D-R-F, one seven six, twenty-three was no longer alone.

9.speaker: NARRATOR
9.text: A letter came from the district court. Not a summons. Not a police notice. One line, on official paper, asking for one document. And Mervyn Aloysius Fonseca had eleven days to produce a piece of paper that had never existed in this world.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Read it again.

9.speaker: sarika
9.text: Sir, I have read it three times.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Read it again.

9.speaker: sarika
9.text: The Registrar requests that a certified copy of the order appointing the presiding officer of the said forum be furnished to this office within eleven days.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Eleven days.

9.speaker: sarika
9.text: Sir, what is this appointing order? I have never filed it in the registry.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: You have never filed it because it is not with the registry.

9.speaker: sarika
9.text: Then where is it, sir?

9.speaker: NARRATOR
9.text: There it was. The question the whole building had been asking for five years, finally asked by the only person in it who did not know the answer.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Go home, Sarika.

9.speaker: sarika
9.text: Sir—

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Go home. And do not sign anything tomorrow.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: You look like a man who has received a letter.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Pandit-ji. I need one thing more.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: You need. Always you need.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: There are old registers. Two thousand nineteen. Section eleven appointments. If one entry were to exist there—

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: Stop.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Nobody reads a nineteen register.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: Stop talking. Right now.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: Do you know what you are asking me? You are asking me to insert a false entry into a court record. That is not a favour. That is forgery, and it is my handwriting, and it is my cupboard.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: I have given you twelve outcomes.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: You have given me nothing! You opened envelopes and you wrote reasons around what was already inside them!

9.speaker: NARRATOR
9.text: And there it was, said out loud for the first time. Twelve envelopes. Twelve disputes. Twelve outcomes, decided before any hearing ever began.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: I wrote reasons. The reasons were sound.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: The reasons were decoration. Every envelope was telling you the answer, and you were only deciding how nicely to say it.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Whose envelopes were they?

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: No questions. That was the price.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: Pandit-ji. Eleven days. Give me one old number and I will never come back here.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: I will not touch your appointment order.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: And bring back the pending list. All thirty-two pages. Tomorrow.

9.speaker: morris
9.text: You are frightened.

9.speaker: pandit
9.text: Nineteen years in that cupboard, Mervyn. Nineteen years nobody asked me one question. And now a registrar is asking questions about a forum that I helped feed.

9.speaker: NARRATOR
9.text: Two men in an empty corridor. Both invisible. Both finished. And only one of them still believed there was a way out.

9.speaker: NARRATOR
9.text: Eleven days. Ten. Nine. And on the eighth day, a builder called Sitaram Dhawale sent word that he wanted a hearing. The biggest one yet.

10.speaker: NARRATOR
10.text: This was the day he had built everything for. A full room. Fourteen people standing at the back. And in the last row, a boy in his first year of law college, watching his father work.

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Papa, there is no place to sit.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Then stand at the back and watch. Do not speak once.

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Mummy said I should not come.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Your mother has never seen me work.

10.speaker: sarika
10.text: Matter number two hundred and four. Parties to enter.

10.speaker: NARRATOR
10.text: She called it flatly. No volume. No pride. Fourteen months ago he had made her practise that sentence until the tyre shop could hear it.

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: Sir. Before the parties argue, I have handed your clerk a working draft.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: A working draft of what?

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: Of the outcome. It saves the forum's time.

10.speaker: NARRATOR
10.text: A prewritten order. In a packed room. Handed across a desk like a tea bill.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Take it back.

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: Sir, look at page two before you decide anything.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Page two of your draft?

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: No, sir. Page two of the other bundle. Twelve awards. Two thousand nineteen to two thousand twenty-three. All signed by you.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Where did you get those?

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: The same place you got your instructions, sir.

10.speaker: NARRATOR
10.text: The envelopes. Twelve sealed envelopes, from a registry clerk who would not take cash. And Mervyn understood, four years too late, whose hand had been inside them.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Get out of my forum.

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: Your forum. Yes. Above my friend's tyre shop, whose rent I have been paying since April.

10.speaker: dhawale
10.text: The western parcel. Two crore ten lakh. You will hear the matter fully, you will write your excellent reasons, and the parcel will come to me.

10.speaker: advocate
10.text: Sir, I object. I object on the record, in front of this entire room.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Counsel—

10.speaker: advocate
10.text: For four years I have watched you do correct work in a room you had no right to sit in. Do not let this be the last order anybody remembers.

10.speaker: sarika
10.text: Sir. I will not certify this one.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Sarika, call the next exhibit.

10.speaker: sarika
10.text: I said I will not certify it. In front of everybody. Write it in the register.

10.speaker: NARRATOR
10.text: A twenty-three year old girl with a twelfth standard certificate, standing up in a full room, refusing to sign. And the presiding officer continued the hearing.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: The forum notes the clerk's objection. The hearing continues.

10.speaker: NARRATOR
10.text: Two hours later, the room was empty. The chairs were stacked. And one boy was still standing at the back.
10.sfx_cue: room emptying, chairs stacking, then quiet

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Papa.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: You should have gone home with your mother.

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: In the second semester we did the Arbitration Act.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Good. It is a useful subject.

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Section eleven. Appointment of arbitrator.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Tejas—

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Then you know an arbitrator can conduct proceedings outside a courthouse.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Yes.

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Yes. After somebody lawfully appoints him.

10.speaker: morris
10.text: Tejas—

10.speaker: tejas
10.text: Papa. Which court appointed you?

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: It took twenty-two years of experience, four days of work, and one man who refused to be hurried. And at the end of it, Harshad Kotak had the only weapon that had ever mattered in this story. He had proof of a negative.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Bring the current empanelment. Then the retired. Then section eleven, all five years.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: Sir, we did this four days back.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: We did it once. Once is an opinion. Three times is a record.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: Thirty-four awards had now come into that registry. Thirty-four. From landlords, brothers, contractors, builders. Every one of them annexed by somebody who believed a court had spoken.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Current empanelment.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: No such name, sir.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Retired.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: No such name.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Section eleven appointments.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: No such appointment, sir. And no such tribunal was ever constituted.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: And the case-number series?

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: A-D-R-F is not issued by any court in this state, sir.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Now the last one. The bar council roll.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: Sir?

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: The name. Search the roll.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: Sir... the name is there.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Read the entry.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: Enrolment cancelled. Two thousand seven. No valid degree. Convicted, three months.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: Fifteen years earlier, this same building had already answered this same question about this same man. And then it had forgotten him so completely that he was able to walk out and open a court.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Type the verification note. Four heads. Empanelment, appointment, constitution, numbering. Negative on all four.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: And the awards, sir?

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Index all thirty-four. Certified copies. And prepare a sealed set for the police.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: Sir, once this goes... those thirty-four families.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: Yes.

11.speaker: RECORDS ASSISTANT
11.text: Some of them got justice, sir. People are saying it in the district.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: I know what people are saying.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: A genuine dispute does not create a genuine tribunal. If we accept one good order from that room, we accept every bad one. And there is no way for you or me to know which is which.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: He signed it. And in twenty-two years at that desk, it was the first thing Harshad Kotak had ever signed that would take something away from somebody.

11.speaker: khot
11.text: Registrar sahib. This is a large complaint.

11.speaker: hardik
11.text: It is a complete complaint. Verification note, bar record, and thirty-four certified awards.

11.speaker: khot
11.text: IPC one seventy. Pretending to hold office as a public servant. And four nineteen, cheating by personation.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: The staircase above the tyre shop was climbed for the last time at ten minutes past six.

11.speaker: khot
11.text: Madam. Sarika Kamble?

11.speaker: sarika
11.text: Sir, whatever I signed, I signed because—

11.speaker: khot
11.text: Madam, listen to me. You are named as an employee and a witness. Not as an accused.

11.speaker: sarika
11.text: Not as—

11.speaker: khot
11.text: Where are the registers kept?

11.speaker: sarika
11.text: The steel cupboard. Behind the dais. And the certified copies in the blue file.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: She told them everything in ninety seconds. She had been waiting fourteen months to be asked.

11.speaker: tejas
11.text: Papa, there is nowhere else left.

11.speaker: khot
11.text: Sir. Turn towards me. I will read the allegation before we move.

11.speaker: khot
11.text: That you did cheat persons by falsely representing that you held judicial authority, and did thereby induce transfers of property and money.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: He did not argue. He did not explain. He looked once at the black board with the gold letters, and he said only one thing.

11.speaker: morris
11.text: Take the board down before the boy comes tomorrow.

11.speaker: NARRATOR
11.text: Thirty-four awards. Thirty-four families. And by tomorrow morning, every single one of them would be told that the day they won was a day that never happened.

12.speaker: NARRATOR
12.text: They offered him a way out. Name every order. Call each one worthless. Say the words, and the charge becomes smaller, the bail becomes easier, and a man of forty-eight might still have a life at the end of it. Thirty-three times, he said the words.
12.sfx_cue: interview room, tube light hum, recorder click

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Name every award, describe it truthfully, and the prosecution will record your cooperation.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: You want me to condemn all of them before any trial.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: I want a complete list and a truthful description of your authority.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: There was no court appointment. That part the record has already established.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Then why do you need me at all?

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Because thirty-four papers changed thirty-four lives, and your handwriting is on all of them.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Some of those disputes were genuine.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: A genuine dispute does not create a genuine tribunal.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: The parties came voluntarily.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Some did. Some were told that a presiding officer had summoned them.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: I never once used the district court's name.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: You used its language. Its procedure. Its appearance.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Language belongs to no court.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Authority does.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Start with matter one. Speak clearly for the recorder.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Matter one. A housing lockout. Six thousand rupees withheld.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Did the landlord pay because of your paper?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: He restored the key and paid six thousand rupees.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Then state whether it had judicial force.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: It did not have judicial force.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Matter two.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: A supplier recovered forty-two thousand from a contractor. No judicial force.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Matter three.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Possession of a rented storeroom. No judicial force.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Matter four.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Seventeen thousand five hundred rupees. No judicial force.

12.speaker: NARRATOR
12.text: He named payments. Shops. Rooms. Parcels of land. Five years of a man's entire life, taken apart one line at a time, in his own voice, for the recorder.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Were any of those outcomes dictated through sealed envelopes?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Not the first five. From matter nine.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: And what did you receive for them?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Access to the pending list.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: So that you could select disputes which had not reached a real court.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: So that I could avoid conflicting proceedings.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: A very careful description of the same concealment.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: You asked for truth. Not for humiliation.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: The truth is not responsible for your humiliation.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Matter twenty-two.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: A vehicle, after payment of one lakh twelve thousand. No judicial force.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Matter twenty-three.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: A family loan. Eight thousand monthly. No judicial force.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Matter twenty-four.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Land access. Between a sister and a brother.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Full description.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: The sister held an equal recorded share. Her brother controlled both keys.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: For how long?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Eleven years.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: And your award?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Access and possession according to her recorded share. No lease of the western half.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Did the brother comply?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: He gave her both keys.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Then complete the statement. The award had no judicial force.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Next matter.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: No. Finish matter twenty-four.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: The recorded share was hers.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: That may be true. Your authority was not.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Her brother obeyed.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Because he believed a court had spoken.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: For eleven years, nobody else spoke for her.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: She never filed in the district court.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: She could not wait another eleven years to be heard.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Mr Fonseca. This interview is not deciding a land dispute.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: That room decided it.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: That room was not a court.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: It listened when the court had not.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: If I say it — what happens to her keys?

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: The parties will be notified that the award has no legal authority.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Her brother will take them back.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: He may seek lawful determination.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: He held everything for eleven years without one.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: You are not protecting her title by refusing.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: I am protecting the one day she was believed.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: That sentence will not help your bail application.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Then leave it out.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: The list must be complete.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: It is complete through matter twenty-three.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: And matter twenty-four?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: I will not call that judgment worthless.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: It was not a judgment.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: She stood in front of me with eleven years of crop accounts in a school notebook. He had both keys.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: None of that appointed you.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: No.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Then state it.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: No.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Understand the cost. I am recording partial cooperation, refusal to identify all awards as unauthorised, and continuing assertion of judicial power.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Record it.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: The narrower allegation may no longer be available to you.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Record that also.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Why preserve one lie, after admitting thirty-three?

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Because that one made a man return keys he had no right to keep.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: You do not get to decide which false authority becomes noble.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: No. I decided when it cost me nothing. I am deciding this one when it costs me everything.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Interview suspended. Time, six forty-two.

12.speaker: NARRATOR
12.text: The incomplete list went into the police file. Matter twenty-four did not.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: Registrar sahib. Should the sister be contacted tonight?

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Not without a formal notice and a complete verified copy.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: The brother may hear of the arrest first.

12.speaker: hardik
12.text: Then we move carefully.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Do not call her.

12.speaker: khot
12.text: That decision is no longer yours, sir.

12.speaker: morris
12.text: Please. Let her keep one night.

12.speaker: NARRATOR
12.text: Across town, in a lane where every door had been open, Manjula Gaikwad locked the western gate with one key, and the house with the other.
12.sfx_cue: village lane at night, gate closing, lock turning

12.speaker: NARRATOR
12.text: She still held both keys. Nobody had told her anything.

12.speaker: NARRATOR
12.text: And somewhere in that district, thirty-three other people were about to receive a notice — every one of them with a story of their own, and not one of them knowing how it ended.
